evidence_items.claim: Pauline authorship of Galatians is a strong critical consensus, while an unnamed secretary or scribal assistant remains possible.
Galatians 6:11 calls attention to Paul's large letters written with his own hand, plausibly marking an autograph section but not proving why the letters were large.
Paul opposes circumcision for gentile addressees as a crisis of obligation and allegiance; this is not a blanket condemnation of Jewish circumcision or a warrant for anti-circumcision coercion.
The closing contrast denies that circumcision or uncircumcision is decisive and centers boasting in the Messiah's cross and new creation.
Israel of God in Galatians 6:16 may name Jewish Christ-followers, the whole Messiah assembly, Israel more broadly, or another qualified group; grammar and context have not produced consensus.
Paul's marks likely refer to bodily scars associated with service to Jesus and persecution, but branding, ownership, stigma, devotional, and medical reconstructions remain debated.
The letter indicates teachers pressing circumcision and Torah obligation, but their number, origin, self-description, motives, and full program cannot be recovered from Paul's polemic alone.
Galatians instructs people who are spiritual to restore a transgressor gently while watching themselves and bearing burdens; it does not prescribe public humiliation or unchecked discipline.

Galatians combines letter conventions with rebuke, curse, autobiography, scriptural argument, allegory, exhortation, warning, and autograph; assignment to one classical rhetorical species is disputed.
Sowing and reaping in Galatians 6 is an ethical-eschatological analogy about perseverance in communal good, not a formula guaranteeing financial profit.
Galatians 6:6 calls learners to share good things with the one teaching; the scope is debated and cannot license financial extraction or prosperity promises.
Paul warns addressees considering circumcision that the act entails whole-Torah obligation within their present rival-teacher conflict.

evidence_items.claim: Paul is the sole named sender; possible scribal assistance should not be converted into a named coauthor or used to erase collaborative letter production.
Paul's opponents must be reconstructed through his adversarial rhetoric; calling them one settled Jewish-Christian party confuses a scholarly model with direct evidence.

Gentle restoration in Galatians 6 requires self-watch and burden-bearing; it must not become public shaming, authoritarian discipline, coerced confession, surveillance, or forced reconciliation without safety and repair.

Bearing one another's burdens and carrying one's own load are adjacent but use different terms; interpretation should preserve mutual aid and responsible self-assessment rather than weaponizing either.
Sharing all good things with a teacher supports reciprocity but supplies no tithe rate, prosperity promise, collection pressure, leader entitlement, or exemption from financial accountability.
God is not mocked and sowing-reaping language must not be used for victim blame, health-and-wealth promises, disability stigma, disaster explanation, or coercive fundraising.
Doing good especially to the household of faith creates a community priority without permitting sectarian neglect, ethnic favoritism, or refusal of aid to outsiders.
Large letters may signal emphasis, handwriting, eyesight, or another circumstance; Galatians 6:11 cannot diagnose Paul or prove the size of the entire original letter.
Boasting only in the cross is theological rhetoric about allegiance and status; it must not glorify suffering, demand abuse endurance, or turn trauma into spiritual prestige.
New creation in Galatians 6:15 carries cosmic and communal possibilities; it is not merely private self-improvement or permission to discard embodied, Jewish, or ecological histories.

Israel of God remains grammatically and theologically disputed; using it as an uncomplicated synonym for the church can fuel supersessionism, while excluding every gentile is also an argued inference.
Paul's marks likely evoke scars or branding, but Paul's marks must not romanticize trauma, stigmatize disability, promote medical neglect, or demand that leaders prove authority through suffering.
Grace in the closing benediction addresses siblings without resolving every dispute; benediction must not be used to bypass accountability, safety, restitution, or repair.

Galatians cannot authorize nationalism, ethnic supremacy, conspiracy theories, partisan capture, colonial mission, forced conversion, religious violence, or ecological neglect; those modern systems require independent ethical evaluation.
Those called spiritual are told to restore a person caught in transgression with gentleness while watching themselves against temptation.
